reading: Each solid square is replaced, in place and concentrically, by the next size in the cycle 9->7->5->3->1->9: squares lose their outer ring, and a single cell grows into a 9x9 square centred on it.

slots.subject: each single-colour solid square object
slots.size_rule: side n becomes n-2; side 1 becomes 9

why: every output square has the input square's colour and centre and side (n-2), or 9 when n=1

reading: Every object loses the cells in the two leftmost columns of its bounding box (they become background); objects two columns wide vanish.

new_rows.name: left2
new_rows.datalog:
ominx(O, min(X)) :- obj(O, Y, X), cell(Y, X, C).
left2(Y, X) :- obj(O, Y, X), cell(Y, X, C), ominx(O, M), L = M + 2, X < L.

why: exactly the object cells in the first two columns of each object's box turn to background colour 8; nothing else changes

reading: Two overlapping shapes: the one that is partly hidden is brought to the front, so the overlap cells take the colour of the occluded shape and it is shown complete.
verb: swap layering (bring occluded shape to front)

slots.subject: the incomplete (occluded) shape
slots.completion: its full shape (rectangle, line or diagonal) as implied by its visible part
slots.overlap: cells where the complete shape covers the occluder are recoloured to the occluded shape's colour

why: after the change the previously occluded shape is a complete rectangle/line and the other shape loses exactly the overlap cells

reading: Each colour-4 rectangle contains N dots of some colour c; draw a border of colour c around the rectangle with thickness N.

slots.subject: each 4-rectangle with its inner dots
slots.colour: the colour of the inner dots
slots.place: ring of that thickness around the rectangle's box, on background cells

why: every rectangle is surrounded by a solid ring whose colour is its dot colour and whose width equals its dot count
invariants: the rectangles and their dots unchanged

reading: Plus-shaped objects whose centres lie on a common diagonal are joined by a diagonal line of colour 2 drawn on the background cells between them.

slots.subject: pairs of plus objects with centres on the same diagonal
slots.line: diagonal from centre to centre, background cells only

why: every 2 cell lies on the diagonal between two plus centres that are diagonally aligned, and every such pair is joined

reading: Each bar standing on the bottom edge is lifted straight up by a distance equal to its own height.
why: every object keeps its shape and column span and its rows shift up by its height

reading: The whole grid is filled with its most common colour.

slots.colour: the most frequent colour of the input

why: the output is uniform and its colour is the input's majority colour

reading: Small pieces attached to a colour-9 hub slide away from the hub, in the direction they stick out from it, until they reach the grid border; the 9 hub stays.
verb: push pieces away from hub to border

slots.subject: each non-9 object touching the hub
slots.direction: from the touching 9 cell toward the object (up/down/left/right)

why: each piece keeps its shape and ends touching the border on the side it pointed to; hub unchanged

reading: The 3-shape slides toward the 2-line until it touches it, and a full line of colour 8 is drawn alongside the 3-shape's box on the side away from the 2-line.
verb: slide to wall and mark the back

slots.subject: the colour-3 shape (largest object)
slots.target: the colour-2 full line; move until contact
slots.mark: full line of colour 8 parallel to the 2-line, adjacent to the moved shape's box on the far side

why: the 3-shape keeps its shape and touches the 2-line; the 8 line is directly behind it

reading: A 2x2 colour key sits in a corner beyond the 8 bars; the square work area is split into four quadrants and each dot takes the key colour at the matching quadrant position.

slots.key: the 2x2 block of colours in the corner of the 8 bars
slots.region: the square area bounded by the 8 bars, cut into 2x2 equal quadrants
slots.subject: every dot in the area
slots.colour: key cell in the same relative quadrant

why: every dot's new colour equals the key cell whose position matches the dot's quadrant
